proposed.description: Horde Groupware: find the authentication backend before trusting the login page Horde Groupware bundles webmail, calendars, contacts, tasks, notes, and file tools. Its login page can be the entrance to several applications and identity sources. Horde does not provide a universal default administrator account; the configured authentication backend decides which accounts exist and which ones are administrators. Query evidence ZoomEye returned 17 matches for title="Horde Groupware" , zero for app="Horde Groupware" , 203 for http.body="Horde Groupware" , and 2,995 for http.body="/horde/imp" . All queries used sub_type=all , page 1, pagesize 1. The /horde/imp marker is useful because IMP is a Horde webmail component, but it is still a body match. A page can mention the path or serve a stale template. The exact title count is smaller and should be treated as a narrow candidate list. Neither observation proves that setup mode, a weak backend, or an administrator account is exposed. Horde installation documentation warns that a fresh setup can be accessible without a password until a real authentication backend and administrator list are configured. That is a deployment state to check, not something an outside search can prove. proposed.author: Zippic
proposed.description: A QR code can look intact in a compressed event flyer and still fail on a phone. The three corner markers remain visible, the text around it looks acceptable, and the file passes the upload limit. Yet the camera cannot reliably separate the smaller squares that carry the data. That makes a QR-bearing image a different optimization problem from an ordinary photograph. Visual similarity is useful, but successful decoding of the final delivered image is the acceptance test. A smaller file is not an improvement if people cannot use it. Protect the grid and its quiet zone The small squares in a QR code are called modules. A scanner needs to distinguish their positions and identify the symbol against its surroundings. DENSO WAVE, the developer of QR Code, specifies a clear margin four modules wide on every side of a standard QR code. That margin is the quiet zone, not disposable whitespace. Cropping tightly around the black pattern removes useful structure. Placing a caption, border, or busy photograph immediately against it can also interfere with detection. Preserve the quiet zone as part of the asset when placing a code in a flyer or slide. An opaque light background is more predictable than transparency when the destination background may change. proposed.title: Why a QR Code Stops Scanning After Image Compression

proposed.author: EditorDavid
proposed.description: The Register writes that "The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds." In his weekly kernel update post, Torvalds said Linux 7.4 rc2 was a big release partly because it contained code he'd left out of rc1 because he'd been busy and it was already the largest such release in kernel history. But Torvalds said the other reason rc2 was big was "various AI fixes." Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April, developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible. Microsoft, for example, addressed a record 974 flaws in September — its third record fixing spree this year after it whacked 622 flaws in July and 206 in June. Oracle addressed 1,449 flaws in a single month. That's many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI. Torvalds' post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us. "This time around Alexei claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true," he wrote. That's a reference to Alexei Starovoitov, co-creator and lead dev on the Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), the project that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs within the Linux kerne
proposed.title: Linus Torvalds Wonders If Linux's AI-Prompted Patch Flood Has Peaked
